Revelation 11:2: the holy city is trampled 42 months. This is about three and a half years, close to the length of the Roman war from spring AD 67 to August AD 70.
Revelation 13:5-7: the beast is given 42 months and makes war with the saints. No covenant is mentioned.

Futurists answer that Revelation assumes Daniel's framework. They say two periods of 1,260 days add up to the seven-year week, and that Daniel 9:27 itself supplies the covenant. Revelation does not need to repeat it. Many idealists read the time periods as symbols of the whole church age.
Do other biblical time spans, like forty years or forty days, ever contain hidden gaps?

No. Scripture uses forty years for Moses' life stages, the wilderness, judges and kings, and forty days for the flood, Sinai and Jesus' fast. Each is continuous. A stated number of years means a continuous span.

Forty-year spans include Moses in Egypt and in Midian (Acts 7:23, 30), the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2), rest under Othniel, Deborah and Gideon (Judges 3:11; 5:31; 8:28), and Philistine rule (Judges 13:1). They also include Eli (1 Samuel 4:18) and the reigns of Saul, David, Solomon and Joash (Acts 13:21; 2 Samuel 5:4; 1 Kings 11:42; 2 Chronicles 24:1). Ezekiel announces forty years of desolation for Egypt (Ezekiel 29:11-12). Forty-day spans include the flood rains (Genesis 7:12), Moses on Sinai (Exodus 24:18), the spies (Numbers 13:25), Goliath's taunts (1 Samuel 17:16), Elijah's journey (1 Kings 19:8) and Jesus' fast (Matthew 4:2). On the fulfilled reading, none of these contains a hidden pause. Why should Daniel's seventy weeks be the one exception?
Acts 7:23, 30, 36: Moses' 120 years fall into three forties with no gaps (Deuteronomy 34:7).
Numbers 14:34: forty days of spying become forty years of wandering, a year for each day, with no gap.

Dispensationalists accept that those numbers are continuous. But they say Daniel 9 is unique because it splits the weeks (7, 62, 1) and puts events "after" the sixty-two. Some also point to gaps in fulfilment, such as Isaiah 61:2 in Luke 4:19, rather than gaps in a counted span.
What do Jeremiah's seventy years teach us about reading Daniel's seventy weeks?
Daniel prayed because he took Jeremiah's seventy years literally and continuously. Since Daniel 9 begins there, the seventy weeks should be read the same way: consecutive and without gaps.

Daniel 9 opens with Daniel reading Jeremiah. He understood that Jerusalem's desolation would last seventy years (Daniel 9:2; Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10). The captivity let the land enjoy its missed sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34-35, 43; 2 Chronicles 36:21). Daniel did not suspect a hidden gap. As the seventy years neared their end, he prayed for restoration, and God answered with "seventy weeks" (9:24). The pattern of seven sabbath-years and the jubilee (Leviticus 25:1-10) lies behind both numbers. Jacques Doukhan noted that Daniel read Jeremiah's prophecy realistically. Daniel's own weeks should be read the same way. On the fulfilled reading, if God had added a hundred-year pause to the seventy years and still called it seventy, no one would call that faithfulness. The same applies to the seventy weeks.
2 Chronicles 36:21-23: the seventy years end and Cyrus's decree follows in 538 BC.
Leviticus 25:8: seven sabbaths of years make 49 years. This matches Daniel's first "seven weeks" (9:25).

Dispensationalists agree the seventy years were continuous. But they see Daniel 9 as a new revelation with its own structure, including events placed "after" the sixty-two weeks. Some scholars note that the seventy years themselves are counted in different ways (605-536 BC or 586-516 BC).
Does the division into seven weeks, sixty-two weeks and one week justify a gap before the last week?
On the fulfilled reading, no. No one puts a gap between the seven and the sixty-two weeks, so the split alone cannot create one before the seventieth. Moses' life in three forties has no gaps either.

Daniel divides the seventy weeks into seven weeks (49 years), sixty-two weeks (434 years) and one week (7 years). Some argue that this division opens space for a pause. But dispensationalists themselves run the seven and the sixty-two together without a break. They have no reason in the text to treat the last division differently. Moses' 120 years fall into three forties (Acts 7:23, 30; Deuteronomy 34:7), yet no one adds gaps. E. W. Hengstenberg asked how anyone could imagine an interval between the sixty-nine and the one when together they make up the seventy. Milton Terry noted that in Hebrew the plural "seventy weeks" takes a singular verb, "is decreed" (Daniel 9:24). The seventy are treated as one unit.
Daniel 9:24, Hebrew: shavu'im shiv'im nechtak. A plural noun with a singular verb ("is decreed").
7 + 62 + 1 = 70: the parts add up to the stated whole, leaving nothing over for a gap.

Dispensationalists reply that the text places the Messiah's cutting off and the city's destruction "after" the sixty-two weeks (9:26), not "in" the seventieth. This, they say, signals a break. Some amillennialists, such as Meredith Kline, also see the seventieth week as symbolic and stretching across the church age.
Does "prophetic postponement" in other Old Testament texts justify a gap in Daniel 9?
On the fulfilled reading, no. Even if some prophecies are fulfilled in stages, none of the examples involves a stated, counted number of years being stopped and restarted.

Some dispensational scholars, such as Randall Price, argue for "prophetic postponement". In their view many Old Testament prophecies have a partial fulfilment in history and a complete one in the end times, with a gap between. They cite passages such as Isaiah 9:6-7, Isaiah 61:1-2 and Zechariah 9:9-10. On the fulfilled reading, these examples are open to debate. More importantly, none of them contains a numbered time span like "seventy weeks". A prophecy that does not give a timetable may unfold in stages. A prophecy that says exactly how many years will pass cannot be paused without changing its meaning. Daniel 9 is precisely the kind of text where a gap would undo the prophecy's own claim.
Luke 4:18-21: Jesus stops reading before "the day of vengeance". But Isaiah 61 has no number of years.
Daniel 9:24 by contrast states a count: "seventy weeks are decreed".

Dispensationalists answer that if the prophets could leave unmarked gaps between two comings of Christ, Daniel could too. They see verse 26's events, placed "after" the sixty-two weeks but not in the seventieth, as exactly such a gap. Many amillennial and historic premillennial scholars also accept staged fulfilments of prophecy in general.
Does Daniel 9:26 describe a "period between" the sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks?

The text says certain events happen "after" the sixty-two weeks. It does not say "but not in the seventieth". The fulfilled reading says no period of time can sit between two weeks unless the text states one.

Some writers, such as Robert Culver, call it the "one natural interpretation" that verse 26's events belong to a period between the two weeks. In that period God sets Israel aside until a future restoration. But the text never mentions such a period. As Hans LaRondelle noted, it says "after the sixty-two weeks". It does not say "after the sixty-two weeks, but not in the seventieth". The next week naturally follows the sixty-two, as January 1 follows December 31. On the fulfilled reading, the Messiah was cut off early in the seventieth week, which is after the sixty-ninth. That fits the text exactly. To assume a "period between" first and then find it in the text is to argue in a circle.
Daniel 9:26: "after the sixty-two weeks Messiah will be cut off". This is in the seventieth week, which comes right after the sixty-second.
A modern parallel: a 70-week contract has no week between week 69 and week 70 unless the contract says so.

Dispensationalists hold that if the Messiah's death came "in" the seventieth week, the text would say so. They take the destruction of the city, also "after" the sixty-two, as clearly outside the seventieth week, so a gap is already present. Historicists and amillennialists usually agree with the continuous reading.
Does Daniel 9 promise a future restoration of Israel to the land at the end of the seventy weeks?
The text does not mention a later return to the land. Israel was in the land through all seventy weeks and when the temple fell in AD 70. Joshua 21:43-45 also says God fulfilled his land promise.

Daniel prayed about the return from Babylon, and that return happened under Cyrus (Ezra 1:1-4). The seventy weeks that follow are about what God would do for "your people and your holy city". He would finish transgression, atone for sin, bring everlasting righteousness and anoint a most holy place (Daniel 9:24). Then the city and sanctuary would be destroyed (9:26). Nothing in the passage foretells a second return after a long gap. Israel was in the land when the sixty-ninth week ended, when the seventieth began, and when Jerusalem fell. Joshua 21:43-45 says that not one of God's good promises about the land failed. On the fulfilled reading, the seventy weeks end with atonement in Christ, not with a modern political event.
Joshua 21:45: "Not one word failed of all the good things which the LORD had spoken".
Nehemiah 9:7-8: the returned exiles praise God for keeping his land promise to Abraham.

Dispensationalists and many other premillennialists answer that later prophets still promised a future regathering (Ezekiel 36-37; Amos 9:14-15). They say the Abrahamic land promise is eternal (Genesis 17:8). Many also see the modern return of Jews to the land as part of God's purpose, though views differ on how.
Would a future seven-year judgment on Israel mean God punishes the nation twice for the same sin?
The fulfilled reading argues that the judgment for rejecting the Messiah fell in AD 70. Nahum's "distress will not rise up twice" suggests God does not repeat a completed judgment.

Jesus said that the blood of the prophets would be required of "this generation" (Matthew 23:35-36; Luke 11:50-51). He described Jerusalem's fall as "days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled" (Luke 21:22). On the fulfilled reading, that judgment was complete in AD 70. Nahum 1:9 says of God's judgment on Nineveh that "distress will not rise up a second time". The same principle applies here: a completed sentence is not carried out again. To expect a future tribulation in which most of Israel suffers again for the same rejection would mean repeating a judgment Scripture describes as finished. The good news for every generation, Jewish or Gentile, is the open door of Christ (Romans 10:12-13; 11:23).
Luke 21:22: "all things which are written" are fulfilled in those days of vengeance.
Romans 11:23: if they do not continue in unbelief, they will be grafted in. The door stays open.

Futurists reply that the future tribulation is not a second punishment for the cross. They say it is a time of refining that brings Israel to faith (Jeremiah 30:7; Zechariah 13:8-9) and also judges a rebellious world. Nahum 1:9 refers to Assyria. It is not a rule for all future history.
If Jerusalem fell in AD 70, about forty years after the seventieth week, doesn't Daniel 9 need some gap anyway?
No. On the fulfilled reading, the city's destruction was "determined" within the seventy weeks but carried out later, as a sentence is given on one day and carried out on another.

Daniel 9:26 says "desolations are determined". On the fulfilled reading, the decisive cause, the rejection and killing of the Messiah (Acts 3:14-15), happened within the seventy weeks. Its outworking came a generation later. Jesus pronounced the temple "desolate" when he left it (Matthew 23:38), forty years before it fell. He told the women of Jerusalem to weep for their children (Luke 23:27-31). Adam was told he would die "in the day" he ate. He died spiritually that day, and physically later (Genesis 2:17; 5:5). A judge passes sentence on one day and it is carried out later. In addition, if a gap were needed, a forty-year gap within that generation would be more natural than one of two thousand years.
Matthew 23:38: "your house is left to you desolate". This was declared in about AD 30 and carried out in AD 70.
Genesis 2:17 and 5:5: death sentenced "in the day". Adam lived 930 years.

Dispensationalists take this as proof that the prophecy spans more than 490 continuous years, which supports some kind of interval. Critical scholars refer the destruction language to Antiochus's profaning of the temple in 167 BC, so they need no gap.
Was the continuous reading of the seventy weeks the historic view before the 1800s?
Largely, yes. Many Protestant interpreters before the 1800s saw the seventieth week fulfilled in Christ. The future-week view spread through J. N. Darby and the Scofield Reference Bible.

From the Reformation onward, most Protestant commentators held that the seventy weeks ran in sequence to Christ. They taught that Christ confirmed the covenant and ended the sacrifices by his death, and that Jerusalem's ruin followed as a result. This was the main view among the Reformers and the Puritans, and among later writers such as Matthew Henry, E. W. Hengstenberg and Philip Mauro. Details differed, especially the starting decree. John Lightfoot, in the 1600s, summed it up this way: Daniel traces Jerusalem from Cyrus's rebuilding to its destruction by Titus, and John's Revelation begins where Daniel ends. On the fulfilled reading, the future seventieth week is a nineteenth-century innovation tied to Darby's sharp separation of Israel and the church.
John Calvin, Commentary on Daniel 9:27 (1561): Christ confirmed the covenant and abolished the sacrifices.
J. N. Darby (1800-1882) developed the "church parenthesis". The Scofield Reference Bible (1909, 1917) made it widely known.

Futurists point out that some early church writers held a future final week. Irenaeus (about 180) and Hippolytus (about 204) set the last week at the end of the age with the Antichrist. So the view is not purely modern. Historicists also held continuous fulfilment but differed on many details.
If one vision shows events far apart in time, isn't that a kind of gap?
Nebuchadnezzar saw one statue with four kingdoms that followed each other over centuries. That shows sequence, not a pause. Each kingdom followed the last without an empty stretch of time.

Daniel 2 shows four kingdoms in one image, and the stone strikes them all together (Daniel 2:34-35). Yet history spread them over centuries. Babylon fell in 539 BC, Persia in 331 BC, and Greek rule gave way to Rome in the 60s BC. Some argue this shows that prophecy can compress time, so a gap in Daniel 9 is possible. On the fulfilled reading, this confuses compression with interruption. Each kingdom in Daniel 2 follows the one before it in an unbroken line. No time passes with no kingdom in place. Daniel 9 also lists its parts in unbroken sequence (7, 62, 1). The judgment on the statue was announced when Daniel explained the dream, though its fulfilment unfolded over centuries. That is a sentence given and later carried out, not a clock stopped.
539 BC: Babylon falls to Cyrus (Daniel 5:30-31). 331 BC: Persia falls to Alexander at Gaugamela.
63 BC: Pompey takes Jerusalem, and Judea comes under Rome, the fourth kingdom.

Dispensationalists see Daniel 2's stone as striking the toes at Christ's second coming. In their view the toes stand for a future, revived form of the fourth empire, which requires a long gap after ancient Rome. Many other interpreters accept continuity but differ on whether the fourth kingdom is Rome or Greece.
When a volcano or a great earthquake strikes, is it a sign that the end of the world is near?
Not by itself. Great disasters have struck every century. People who lived through them often felt the end had come, yet the world went on.

On the fulfilled reading, a disaster is not a prophetic clock. In June 1991 Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted. Some who lived near it said they thought it was the end of the world. In January 1995 the Kobe earthquake in Japan killed more than 6,000 people, and some survivors said the same. But Pinatubo had erupted before, about five centuries earlier, and people then surely felt the same fear. Solomon reminds us that there is nothing new under the sun. Jesus also said that wars and earthquakes are 'not yet the end' (Matthew 24:6). The signs he gave were tied to his own generation. So a disaster today is a real warning to repent, but it is not a sign that fixes the date of Christ's return.
Mount Pinatubo, June 1991: one of the largest eruptions of the 20th century. Geologists date its previous large eruption to about 500 years earlier.
Kobe (Great Hanshin) earthquake, 17 January 1995: about 6,400 dead. Some survivors told reporters they thought the world was ending.
Ecclesiastes 1:4, 9: one generation goes and another comes; what has happened will happen again.

Many futurist teachers agree that one disaster proves nothing. But they say the rising number and strength of disasters, like birth pains (Matthew 24:8), shows the end is close. Historicists see a long series of judgments through church history. Idealists see such events in every age as reminders of a fallen world awaiting Christ.
If disasters are not end-time signs, do they still carry a message from God?
Yes. Scripture shows God sometimes uses earthquakes and plagues as judgment or warning. Every disaster reminds us that the world is fallen and that we must repent.

This reading keeps a moral meaning for disasters while denying that they date the end. In Numbers 16 the ground opened and swallowed Korah's rebels. That was a direct judgment. In Amos 4 God sent famine, drought and plague so that Israel would return to him. But Scripture also warns us not to read every disaster as a verdict on its victims. Jesus said the men killed by the tower in Siloam were no worse sinners than others (Luke 13:4-5). He said the man born blind did not suffer because of his own sin or his parents' sin (John 9:1-3). So the right response to a disaster is humble repentance and mercy to the suffering, not date-setting. Eighteenth-century preachers like John Wesley saw earthquakes as calls to repent, not as timetables.
John Wesley's sermon on the causes and cure of earthquakes (1750) followed tremors felt in London. He called hearers to 'prepare to meet' God (Amos 4:12).
In 1756 the colonial preacher Gilbert Tennent saw frequent earthquakes as a hint of great changes, not as proof of Christ's soon return.
Luke 13:1-5: the Galileans killed by Pilate and the eighteen killed at Siloam.

Most Christians of all views agree with this moral reading. Some charismatic and futurist teachers go further. They name specific disasters as God's response to specific national sins, for example policies about Israel. Others warn that such claims go beyond Scripture and can wound victims.
Why does each generation tend to think that its own troubles are uniquely prophetic?
Because we know little of the past. We read our own news as unique when history shows the same troubles again and again.

This reading calls the problem 'generational provincialism'. It is the belief that nothing has prophetic meaning unless it happens to us. Most people know their own decade far better than past centuries. So the wars, plagues and moral decline of today feel unique. But wars, famine and disease have been part of human life since the fall (Genesis 3:17-19). Ecclesiastes says one generation goes and another comes, and there is nothing new under the sun. The cure is to study history and to read prophecy in its own time frame. When we do this, we find that many past generations were just as sure as we are that they were the last. All of them were wrong.
About AD 1000, and again around 1260 and 1500, many in Europe expected the end. Each date passed.
During the Black Death (1347-51) many believed Jesus' words about pestilence were being fulfilled in their day.
Columbus wrote in his Book of Prophecies (about 1501) that the world had only about 150 years left.

Futurists reply that some things really are new: the return of Israel in 1948, global communication and weapons of mass destruction. They argue these make our age different from all earlier ones. Historicists also hold that later generations stand nearer the end of a long prophetic sequence.
Does a mood of decline and pessimism in society prove that the end is near?
No. Europe around 1492 was gloomy and felt it was shrinking. Yet the Reformation, new learning and the spread of the gospel to new lands followed.

On this reading, gloom is a feeling, not a prophecy. A historian of Columbus described Western Europe at the end of 1492 as deeply pessimistic. Christendom was divided, Islam was advancing, the universities were weak, and many escaped into the pagan past. That picture could describe many later ages too. Yet within a generation came the Reformation (1517), a rediscovery of Scripture, and the spread of the gospel to new continents. God often works most when hope seems least. The kingdom is like yeast that slowly fills the dough (Matthew 13:33). Christians should not mistake a dark season for the final hour. Isaiah promised that the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD (Isaiah 11:9).
Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Many in Europe felt Christendom was in retreat.
Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses in 1517, 25 years after 1492.
Matthew 13:31-33: the mustard seed and the yeast show slow, steady growth.

Premillennial teachers often expect things to grow worse before Christ returns. They cite 2 Timothy 3:1-5 and Luke 18:8 ('will he find faith on the earth?'). Amillennialists expect good and evil to grow side by side until the end. Postmillennialists, like this reading, expect the gospel to triumph widely in history.
How can we tell whether an event is a prophetic sign, since generations come and go but the end has not come?
This reading offers four keys: find the time frame, check the historical record, study the historical context, and separate fulfilment from application.

Many earlier Christians were sure that the signs fitted their times. They were wrong. To avoid their mistake, this reading uses four keys. First, notice the time frame. Many prophecies say when they will happen, such as 'this generation' (Matthew 24:34) or 'near' (Revelation 1:3). Second, check history. If a 'sign' has happened in every century, its appearance today proves little. Third, study the historical context. When the time text is clear, look for fulfilment in that period before looking to the future. Fourth, separate fulfilment from application. A prophecy may be fulfilled once, but its lessons apply in every age. The normal rules for reading Scripture still apply. These four are simply the ones most often ignored when prophecy is the subject.
Key 1 applied: Daniel read Jeremiah's 'seventy years' and knew the exile was nearly over (Daniel 9:2).
Key 4 applied: Babylon's fall is fulfilled, yet it still warns proud nations (Psalms 2:10-12).

Futurists also use time texts but read them differently. 'Near' may mean 'certain' or 'next on God's calendar'. 'This generation' may mean the generation that sees the signs. Historicists read prophecy as a continuous outline of church history. Idealists stress the fourth key and say the main purpose of prophecy is timeless application.
Does the Bible give prophecies with fixed time frames, and what do they teach us?
Yes. Many prophecies give exact periods: 400 years, seven years, forty years, seventy years. Each was fulfilled within its time frame, not in later periods of the same length.

Read with the first key, these prophecies show that God means what he says about time. God told Abraham that his offspring would be oppressed in a foreign land for four hundred years (Genesis 15:13). Exodus 12:40-41 records that Israel left Egypt at the end of 430 years, 'on that very day'. Joseph foretold seven years of plenty and seven of famine (Genesis 41:29-30). Later famines are not fulfilments of that word. Israel wandered forty years, a year for each day the spies explored the land (Numbers 14:34). Judah's exile lasted seventy years to repay the land's missed sabbaths (2 Chronicles 36:21). Daniel trusted that number and prayed (Daniel 9:2). Later seventy-year spans do not fulfil Jeremiah. In the same way, prophecies tied to 'this generation' belong to that generation.
Genesis 15:13 and Exodus 12:40-41: 400 years foretold (a round number); 430 years recorded, 'to the very day'.
Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10: seventy years for Babylon. Cyrus allowed the return in 538 BC (Ezra 1:1-4).
Numbers 14:33-34: forty days of spying became forty years of wandering.

Everyone agrees these periods were literal and fulfilled. Futurists add that some prophecies contain gaps or have a near and a far fulfilment, for example Daniel's seventieth week. Some also see 'day-year' patterns that historicists extend to long church-age periods, such as 1,260 years.
Were people in Jesus' day expecting the Messiah because of Daniel's timetable?
Very likely. Simeon, Anna and many others were waiting. False messiahs arose too. Even Roman writers report a common belief that rulers from Judea would arise.

On this reading, Daniel's seventy weeks (Daniel 9:24-25) gave Israel a time frame for Messiah the Prince. The Gospels show a nation on watch. Simeon waited for 'the consolation of Israel' (Luke 2:25). Anna spoke to all who looked for Jerusalem's redemption (Luke 2:38). Crowds wondered if John might be the Christ (Luke 3:15). Gamaliel mentioned Theudas and Judas the Galilean, who drew followers (Acts 5:36-37). Magi from the east came looking for a newborn king (Matthew 2:1-2). Daniel had been a chief of Babylon's wise men (Daniel 2:48), so his writings may have been known in the east. Paul says Christ came 'when the fullness of the time had come' (Galatians 4:4). Jesus himself announced, 'The time is fulfilled' (Mark 1:15).
Tacitus (Histories 5.13) and Suetonius (Vespasian 4) both mention an old, widespread belief that men from Judea would rule the world.
Josephus (Jewish War 6.5.4) says an 'ambiguous oracle' in the Scriptures about a world ruler from their country stirred the Jews to war.
Acts 5:36-37: Theudas and Judas the Galilean led failed movements.

Most interpreters agree that messianic hope was high in the first century. They differ on how exact the calculation was. Some scholars doubt that ordinary people computed Daniel's weeks. They think the hope came from many texts and from Roman oppression. Dispensational writers like Robert Anderson used Daniel 9 to date Palm Sunday to the day.
Did Israel's statehood in 1948 start a prophetic clock, as the 'fig tree' teaching claims?
On this reading, no. Matthew 24:32 says nothing about Israel becoming a nation again. The 1948-1988 timetable built on it has already failed.

Futurist writers saw the need for a time marker. Hal Lindsey taught that the fig tree's new leaves in Matthew 24:32 picture Israel's rebirth in 1948. He then took 'this generation' as the generation that saw it, about forty years, so roughly 1988. The fulfilled reading answers in three ways. First, the text does not mention Israel's nationhood. Jesus used the fig tree as a simple seasonal lesson: when leaves appear, summer is near. Luke adds 'and all the trees' (Luke 21:29). Second, the New Testament never predicts a restored Jewish state. Third, the Old Testament promises of return were fulfilled after the Babylonian exile (Ezra 1:1-4; Nehemiah 1:8-9). So 1948 is a real and important historical event, but Matthew 24 does not date it.
Luke 21:29-31: 'Look at the fig tree, and all the trees.' The lesson is about seasons, not one nation.
1988 passed without the rapture. Edgar Whisenant's book '88 Reasons' used the same 1948 starting point.
Jeremiah 29:10-14: the promised gathering came 'when seventy years are completed'.

Many futurists still see 1948 as the major prophetic event of the modern era. They point to Ezekiel 37, Isaiah 11:11 ('a second time') and Romans 11:25-26. Some now say a generation may be 70, 80 or 100 years. Many amillennial and covenant writers agree that Matthew 24:32 is not about 1948.
If 'this generation' meant Jesus' hearers, what does that mean for wars and earthquakes in our day?
It means the signs in Matthew 24:4-34 were for AD 30-70. Today's wars and earthquakes are real evils, but they are not those prophetic signs.

On the fulfilled reading, the phrase 'this generation' in the Gospels always points to the people Jesus was speaking to (Matthew 11:16; 12:41-45; 23:36). Jesus said all these things would happen before that generation passed away (Matthew 24:34). So the false christs, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution and the gospel to the nations all came in the forty years before Jerusalem fell in AD 70. Israel may still have a future role in God's plan. But that role does not rest on Matthew 24, because Jesus said nothing there about Israel becoming a nation again. When we hear of wars and earthquakes now, we should pray and help. We should not treat them as a countdown.
Matthew 23:36 and 24:34 use the same phrase. The first clearly means Jesus' hearers.
Famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28), about AD 46; earthquake at Philippi (Acts 16:26).
Colossians 1:6, 23: Paul says the gospel had reached 'all the world' by about AD 60.

Dispensational writers often read 'generation' as the generation alive when the end-time signs begin. Others read it as 'race', meaning the Jewish people will survive. Many evangelical scholars (for example R. T. France) agree verse 34 refers to AD 70. They see a shift to the final coming in verse 36.
Was the Black Death a fulfilment of Jesus' words about pestilence?
Many who lived through it thought so. But on this reading Jesus' signs were for his own generation. The Black Death was a terrible event, not the fulfilment of Matthew 24.

The Black Death of 1347-1351 was perhaps the deadliest disaster in recorded history. Modern historians estimate that between a third and a half of Europe's people died, perhaps 25 to 50 million. Survivors felt they were the generation Jesus spoke about. The poet Petrarch wrote in 1349 that later readers would hardly believe that cities were emptied and fields filled with the dead. If any plague could claim to be 'the' sign, it was this one. Yet the end did not come. This shows the danger of reading our own crisis as unique. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus told his disciples to watch for signs within their own lifetime (Luke 21:11, 32), and they saw them. Later plagues are reminders of a fallen world, not prophetic dates.
